metaDescription: Four Midea Cube dehumidifiers from 20 to 50 pints compared by tank size, pump and coverage, so you can pick the right compact cabinet for a basement.
expertTake: The Cube 50-pint with the built-in pump and smart control is the pick for a basement with no floor drain, because the compact cabinet hides a pump and a tank about three times larger than the older cube design. The Cube 35-pint is the value pick for a mid-size basement. If you want a plain rectangular unit with a front bucket, skip the Cube line.
introParagraphs: A cube-shaped dehumidifier trades the usual tall box for a squat, stackable cabinet. The idea is simple: keep the footprint small, make the water tank larger and give owners a way to drain without lifting a bucket.

That layout suits basements where floor space is limited and the machine lives in a corner for months. The decision comes down to the capacity step, whether a pump is needed and how much connectivity you want, since the cabinet shape stays the same across the range.

products.name: Midea Cube 50-Pint Smart Dehumidifier with Pump, 4,500 Sq Ft
products.description:
This is the Cube with the most going for it. A built-in pump moves water through a hose, vertically or across a room, so a basement without a convenient floor drain stops being a problem. The compact cabinet also carries a water tank up to three times larger than the older cube design, which gives you a longer gap between emptyings when you choose the bucket.

Its 50-pint rating and 4,500 square foot coverage sit at the top of the Cube range, fifteen pints above the 35-pint and thirty above the 20-pint. Smart control lets you adjust the target and check status from a phone, and Energy Star certification keeps running cost down. A pump model costs more than the hose-only 50-pint Cube, so you are paying for drain flexibility.

Ownership is mostly about the hose and the filter. Keep the discharge line free of kinks, rinse the filter every few weeks and test the pump when the humid season begins. If you have a floor drain beside the machine, the cheaper hose-only 50-pint does the same drying without a pump to maintain.

products.description:
The hose-only 50-pint Cube is the straightforward version of the top model. It keeps the 50-pint rating and 4,500 square foot coverage but drains by gravity through an included hose rather than a pump. If a floor drain or sump sits at or below the machine, this is the cheaper way into the same drying capacity.

The cabinet stays compact, and the larger tank means you can still run it without a hose for stretches. The listing stresses smaller form with larger capacity, which is the cube idea in a sentence: you get a 50-pint machine that fits where a tall box would not. Against the 35-pint Cube it adds fifteen pints, which decides whether a damp open basement ever reaches its setpoint.

The tradeoff is flexibility. With no pump, the drain must run downhill, so check the layout before ordering. Keep the intake clear of walls, wash the filter regularly and verify the reading with a separate hygrometer.

products.description:
The 35-pint Cube is the middle step and the best match for most mid-size basements. The 3,500 square foot coverage figure matches what some larger-looking units quote, and the cabinet and enlarged tank are the same cube design as the others.

Compared with the 20-pint Cube, it adds fifteen pints, and against the 50-pint it trades capacity for a lower cost and less draw. In a basement with a steady but moderate problem it cycles off between wet spells, which is healthy for the compressor. In a wet unfinished space it would run nonstop and you should step up.

It is easy to live with. The drain hose supports continuous running, the tank gives a fallback and the Energy Star badge keeps the electric bill reasonable. Rinse the filter monthly and keep the room closed to limit the air volume the unit must treat.

products.description:
The 20-pint is the smallest Cube and the one for a bedroom, a bathroom or a small basement room. It is rated for up to 1,500 square feet and keeps the enlarged tank and drain hose of the larger models.

The cost of the small size is capacity: fifteen pints less than the 35-pint and thirty less than the 50-pint. Under the current federal test of 65F and 60% RH, a 20-pint rating is respectable, but it will still run constantly in an open basement. Keep it for a closed room.

It is the lightest and easiest to carry. Use the hose if you cannot empty the tank daily, clean the filter monthly and place it with room to breathe. For a second room, the same cube shape makes it simple to stack storage around it.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Cube range here comes in 20, 35 and 50 pint steps, rated for roughly 1,500, 3,500 and 4,500 square feet. A bedroom or small room suits the 20-pint, a mid-size basement suits the 35-pint and a large or damp space suits the 50-pint. If the room smells musty or shows condensation, go one step up so the unit cycles off instead of running nonstop. Coverage labels assume open floor and a mild problem, so a basement divided by closed doors behaves like several small spaces, and a single machine placed in one room will leave the others damp.

The smart 50-pint Cube has a built-in pump that drains vertically or across the room. The hose-only 50-pint, the 35-pint and the 20-pint rely on gravity. Measure the height from the machine to the drain first, because a pump costs more but solves an uphill layout that gravity cannot. Also check how long the hose run is, since a long horizontal stretch reduces the effective lift of a small pump, and a sagging loop can trap water and slow the flow.

buyingCriteria.criterion: What the larger tank buys you
buyingCriteria.explanation: The cube design advertises a tank up to three times larger than the older design. That means fewer trips if you choose the bucket, but at 50 pints a wet room still fills it fast. Use the hose for continuous running and treat the tank as a backup. A full tank shuts the unit off, so an owner who travels often should plan on a hose or a pump rather than relying on a daily emptying habit that will eventually slip.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Smart control versus a plain panel
buyingCriteria.explanation: Only the 50-pint with pump lists smart control among the Cube listings here. It helps in a second home or a basement you rarely visit. Check that the local controls still hold a setpoint if the network drops. A simple test is to switch the router off for a minute and confirm the unit keeps working toward its target, and a separate hygrometer will show whether the app reading matches the room.

The cube shape keeps the footprint small and the height low, which helps in a corner near a furnace or a laundry sink. Measure the spot, leave a few inches of clearance at the intake and avoid stacking boxes against the cabinet. A unit with blocked airflow looks weak when it is really mis-placed. Setting it on a small riser keeps it off damp concrete, and keeping the cabinet level helps the bucket float switch read correctly, which prevents false full-tank shutoffs.

Every Cube listed here carries Energy Star certification, which signals lower consumption per pint. Over a humid summer a right-sized machine that cycles off uses less power than one running flat out. Sizing correctly matters more than any badge. Running the machine on a schedule during the humid part of the day and letting the room coast overnight is another way to trim the bill without losing control of the humidity.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity ladder
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the 20, 35 and 50 pint steps and how they map to rooms. Seeing the capacities side by side lets a buyer pick the smallest cube that covers the room. We treated ratings as spec sheet figures, not measurements, and we asked whether the fifteen pint gaps between steps are large enough to change how a damp room behaves.

howWeEvaluated.title: Drain flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the pump on the smart 50-pint with the gravity hose on the others. Because it lifts water to a distant drain, the pump model suits awkward layouts best. A hose in the box scored well for simple installs. We also considered what happens when the hose is blocked, since a unit that fails quietly into a bucket is easier to live with than one that overflows onto a floor.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cabinet and tank
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the compact cube shape and the advertised larger tank. A smaller footprint helps tight basements. We noted that a bigger tank helps only when you cannot use a hose. We also weighed how the low cube profile affects airflow clearance, since a compact body can be pushed too close to a wall.

howWeEvaluated.title: Smart features
howWeEvaluated.description: We assessed smart control on the pump model and the lack of it on the others. App control helps remote spaces. Local control that works without the network is the baseline. Because only one Cube here has the app, we did not treat smart features as a reason to overpay for a small room.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value across the range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared relative price tiers from the 20-pint at the low end to the pump model at the top. All four carry Energy Star. Buying the smallest cube that handles the room gives the best value.

maintenance.why: When the cube's filter fills with dust, air barely reaches the coil and frost becomes more likely. Rinse and dry it fully before reinstalling, and never refit it damp.
Standing water grows slime and odor that ends up in the room air. Mild soap and a rinse prevent it.
A pump that sits idle through a dry winter can stick. Run a cycle and watch the discharge until the flow is steady.
Kinks and sediment stop flow and cause overflow. Confirm the hose end is secured at the drain.
Dust cuts heat transfer and efficiency, and a lint-packed coil is the usual reason a unit slows by its third summer. Unplug first.

faq.q: Which Midea Cube size do I need?
faq.a: A bedroom or small room suits the 20-pint, a mid-size basement suits the 35-pint and a large or damp basement suits a 50-pint. If the space smells musty or shows condensation, go one step up so the unit cycles off instead of running constantly.

faq.q: Is the pump model worth it?
faq.a: Yes when the drain is above the machine or far from it. With a floor drain nearby, the hose-only 50-pint does the same drying with one fewer part to fail.

faq.q: What is special about a cube design?
faq.a: The cabinet is compact and low, and the tank is advertised as up to three times larger than the older design. It is meant to fit tight spots and cut how often you empty the bucket.

faq.q: Do these work in a cool basement?
faq.a: Compressor units lose output near 65F as the coil frosts. Size up a step if the space stays cold, and check the manual for the low-temperature behavior of your model. In a basement that sits near 55F for months, a gentle source of heat or a different technology may do better than a larger compressor unit.

Expect the compressor in a cube to last roughly 5 to 10 years. Cleaning the filter and coil and avoiding an undersized unit are the main levers. A unit that runs flat out in a room it is too small for wears its compressor faster than one that cycles off between wet spells.

Set the Cube for roughly 45 percent. Sustained readings past 60 percent feed mildew and dust mites, and a room pushed below 30 percent turns dry and static-prone. Because the sensor sits right at the unit, a cheap meter in the far corner shows whether the whole room has dried out.
